ABSTRACT
Biomass-derived porous carbon (PC) has emerged as a promising candidate for electrode materials in energy 
storage applications, effective pretreatment of the precursor is a key strategy for enhancing the electrochemical 
performance of PC. However, challenges remain in achieving this goal through environmentally friendly, simple, 
and efficient methods. In this paper, a dual-frequency ultrasonic-assisted enzymolysis strategy combined with 
carbonization-activation method was proposed to prepare high-performance garlic peel-derived PC (DUGPC) for 
supercapacitors. Gentle and effective sonobiocatalysis facilitates microstructural regulation and composition 
management of the precursor, granting DUGPC an impressive specific surface area (SSA, 3006 m
2
/g), improved 
pore distribution, low metal impurity content (less than 100 ppm) and high wettability. As anticipated, DUGPC 
demonstrates excellent specific capacitance (408.77 F/g at 1 A/g) and rate performance (retention is 81.8 % at 
50 A/g) surpassing most recently reported biomass-based PCs. In addition, the assembled aqueous symmetric 
supercapacitor achieves an excellent energy density of 15.78 Wh kg

Significantly, this dual-frequency ultrasonic-assisted enzymolysis strategy is expected to be applicable to various 
biomass wastes and promotes the high-value utilization of biomass in the field of energy storage.
1. Introduction
With the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, the demand 
for energy storage devices continues to emerge in this process due to the 
intermittency of certain clean energy sources, such as wind and solar 
power [1 – 5] . Different from the generally short service life and safety 
risks of batteries, supercapacitors have gradually become one of the 
most promising energy storage technology solutions due to their merits 
of outstanding power density, long cycle life and high reliability [6,7] . 
Electrode materials are a critical component of supercapacitors which 
determine their performance, and porous carbon (PC) has become the 
mainstream choice due to its large specific surface area (SSA), abundant 
source, low price and stable chemical properties [8 – 10] . Biomass, 
including plants, animals and their biodegradable components, is 
considered one of the sustainable and environmentally friendly 
candidates for commercially viable PC precursors [8,11] .
Due to their natural micro-layered structure, PCs with well- 
developed pore structure can typically be obtained from biomass 
(such as scallion peel [12] , sorghum [13] , feather finger grass flower 
[14] , corn straw [15] and walnut shell [16] , etc.) through chemical 
activation, eliminating the need for expensive template methods. 
However, most natural plant cell walls are primarily composed of lignin, 
cellulose and hemicellulose. Lignin serves as a binder, forming a stable 
cross-linked structure between cellulose and hemicellulose. This rigid 
structure, along with its barrier effect, impedes the infiltration of acti -
vators during the carbonization-activation process, resulting in limited 
activation efficiency and porosity [17,18] . Consequently, the micro -
structure of customized precursors before carbonization-activation 
through pretreatment, especially chemical pretreatment, has been 
extensively studied. For example, Yakaboylu et al. used KOH aqueous

chemical pretreatment is effective, biological pretreatment (degrada -
tion) is a notably greener, more sustainable, and simpler approach.
At present, many researchers have reported biodegradation based on 
fungi to prepare PCs, including yeast [21] , Pleurotus ostreatus [22] , 
Neurospora crassa [23] and Trichoderma [24] . However, the harsh cul -
ture conditions and environmental factors affecting microorganisms 
have led to increased interest in enzymes with similar effects, such as 
cellulase and amylase. For instance, Peng et al. treated wood with 
cellulase to form a large number of prefabricated micropores to prepare 
layered porous carbon plates, which exhibited excellent catalytic ac -
tivity in oxygen reduction and oxygen evolution reactions [25] . Wang 
et al. developed carbon materials from cottonseed meal using a 
straightforward enzymolysis strategy with cellulase, the optimized PC 
has a multistage porous structure with high O doping and delivers a high 
specific capacitance of 364 F/g [26] . These findings suggest that cellu -
lase pretreatment enhances the porosity of PCs while offering the ad -
vantages of being green and scalable. Additionally, ultrasound, a 
common enhancement technology in the biological field, is widely 
employed to assist in processes such as organic solvent extraction and 
enzymolysis, improving extraction efficiency and yielding greater 
product quantities [27 – 29] . Nevertheless, there have been few studies 
on the preparation of high-performance PC from biomass using 
ultrasonic-cellulase synergistic pretreatment to date.
Shandong is the leading garlic-producing province in China, with an 
annual output of approximately 4 million tons. It has been reported that 
solid waste, such as garlic peels generated during garlic production, 
accounts for about 22 – 27 % of the total output [30] . Therefore, efficient 
disposal and utilization methods for this waste are urgently needed. In 
this study, we utilized garlic peels as a carbon source to prepare PCs with 
ultra-high SSA as a supercapacitor electrode, employing a dual- 
frequency ultrasonic-assisted enzymolysis strategy. The effects of enzy -
molysis temperature and ultrasonic frequency on the performance of 
PCs were analyzed, and the potential synergistic mechanism of ultra -
sound and cellulase pore-forming was elucidated in this paper. Hence, 
the resulting PC exhibits ultrahigh SSA, competitive capacitive perfor -
mance and energy density that exceed those of previously reported 
biomass-based PCs. Overall, the ultrasound-assisted enzymolysis strat -
egy proposed in this work is expected to be extended to common plant 
precursors, and holds significant promise for developing high- 
performance energy storage materials with controlled pore structures.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials
The raw material (garlic peel) was a thin layer that wraps around the 
garlic clove and sourced from the plantations in Shanghe County, Jinan 
City, Shandong Province. Unless otherwise specified, deionized water 
was used throughout entire experiment, and analytical reagents (KOH, 
HCl and so on) were supplied by Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., 
China. Cellulase (50 U/mg, obtained from Shanghai yuanye Bio- 
Technology Co., Ltd) was produced through the fermentation of Tri -
choderma viride and other excellent strains. The inert protective gas 
utilized in the experiment is high-purity nitrogen ( > 99.999 %) provided 
by Jinan Deyang Special Gas Co., Ltd. (Shandong, China), and the 
single/dual-frequency ultrasonic generator is a laboratory ultrasonic 
cleaner manufactured by Yunyi Ultrasonic (Shenzhen) Co., LTD (China).
2.2. Fabrication of garlic peel-based PC
2.2.1. Cellulase extraction pretreatment
The washed garlic peel was placed in a drying oven at 105 
◦
C for 24 h 
to facilitate crushing. After drying, the garlic peel was processed in a 
crusher for 3 min and then passed through an 80-mesh sieve to obtain a 
powder with a particle size of less than 178 μ m. Next, 5.0 g of garlic peel 
powder was added to a buffer containing 0.5 g of cellulase and main -
tained at a constant temperature (45, 50, 55 ℃ ) for 30 min (solid – liquid 
ratio: 1:40 g/mL, pH: 5.5). Following centrifugal filtration, the cellulase 
was recovered, while the solid residue was washed to neutral pH and 
dried at 105 ℃ for 12 h.
2.2.2. Single-frequency ultrasonic-assisted cellulase pretreatment
The washing, drying, crushing, filtration and other processes for 
garlic peel were consistent with those described in section 2.2.1 . How -
ever, the cellulase extraction pretreatment process was conducted in a 
constant-temperature ultrasonic bath for 30 min (ultrasonic power: 240 
W, ultrasonic frequency: 28/40 kHz).
2.2.3. Dual-frequency ultrasonic-assisted cellulase pretreatment
The pretreatment method is the same as described in section 2.2.2 , 
but the ultrasonic frequency is set to 28 kHz + 40 kHz.
2.2.4. Carbonization-activation process of residue
The dried residue was carbonized in a tube furnace at 600 
◦
C (5 
◦
C/ 
min) for 2 h, then mixed with KOH in an atmospheric furnace at a mass 
ratio of 1:4 and activated at 800 
◦
C (5 
◦
C/min) for 2 h. Finally, the 
activated product was washed with 1 M HCl until the pH reached 6 – 7 
and dried at 105 
◦
C for 24 h to obtain the final sample. Specifically, the 
PC prepared from garlic peel pretreated with cellulase was designated as 
CGPC-X, where X represents the enzymolysis temperature. The PC pre -
pared using single and dual-frequency ultrasound-assisted enzymolysis 
pretreatment were named SUGPC-Y (where Y represents the ultrasonic 
frequency) and DUGPC, respectively. Meanwhile, the PC prepared using 
the direct carbonization-activation method served as the control group 
(GPC).
2.3. Characterization
The SUPRATM 55 scanning electron microscope (SEM, Carl Zeiss AG, 
Germany) and transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEOL JEM-2100 
F, Japan) were used to observe the micromorphology and microstruc -
ture of PCs. The specific surface and pore size analyzer (JW-BK132F, 
JWGB, China) was performed to determine the structural parameters of 
samples. Precisely, the SSA, total pore volume (V
T
) and micropore vol -
ume (V
micro
) were calculated by Bruner-Emmet-Teller (BET) method, 
Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) method and t-plot method respectively. 
Moreover, the measurement of micropores was based on the Horvath- 
Kawazoe (HK) method while the distribution of mesopores and macro -
pores was analyzed according to the BJH method. The phase composi -
tion, structure and crystallinity of samples were characterized by X-ray 
diffraction (XRD, Rigaku D/MAX-2500PC, λ = 1.5406) and Raman 
spectroscopy (Renishaw/RM2000, 514 nm). The element composition 
and surface chemical properties of PCs were conducted by X-ray 
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo/ESCALAB 250 XI). The hy -
drophilicity of PCs was measured by an optical surface tensiometer 
(Theta Flex, Biolin, Sweden) equipped with a GigE zoom digital camera 
(3009 fps). Meanwhile, the metal impurities content of the samples was 
determined by an inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (ICP- 
MS, Agilent 7700, USA).
2.4. Electrochemical measurements
Firstly, PC, polytetrafluoroethylene emulsion (PTFE, 60 wt%) and 
conductive graphite were mixed at a mass ratio of 80:10:10 in ethanol to 
prepare the slurry. For the two-electrode system, the evenly dispersed 
slurry (no less than 4 mg of active material) was coated on a circular 
nickel foam with a diameter of 16.2 mm to form the electrode sheet. 
After drying for 12 h at 80 ℃ in a vacuum drying oven, the electrode

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Selection of enzymolysis temperature and ultrasonic frequency
Temperature and pH are important factors that affect the specificity 
and decomposition efficiency of enzymes for different substrates, and 
they have been reported to have synergistic effects [31,32] . Therefore, it 
is essential to determine the optimal enzymolysis temperature at the 
corresponding pH for to exert the activity of cellulase. Herein, this study 
investigated the effect of enzymolysis temperature on the properties of 
garlic peel-based PC under the condition of pH fixed at 5.5. As can be 
seen from Fig. S1 and Table S1 , both SSA and pore volume of samples 
reach the maximum value when the enzymolysis temperature is 50 ℃ , 
and the corresponding specific capacitance of samples also shows the 
same trend ( Fig. S2 & Table S2 ), indicating that the activity of cellulase 
is the highest at 50 ℃ when pH was 5.5. Consequently, in the next 
exploration of the optimum ultrasonic frequency, the enzymolysis 
temperature is determined to be 50 ℃ .
It can be inferred from Fig. S3 and Table S3 that SSA and pore volume 
of DUGPC prepared by dual-frequency ultrasound-assisted enzymolysis 
are the largest, and 40 kHz is superior to 28 kHz under single frequency 
conditions. This may be due to the fact that oscillation of the cavitation 
bubble in the dual-frequency ultrasonic field is more unstable than that 
in the single-frequency ultrasonic field, and it is easier to collapse 
[33 – 35] . Therefore, dual-frequency ultrasound (28 kHz + 40 kHz) 
produces a stronger cavitation effect than single-frequency ultrasound at 
the same time, thus promoting the enzymatic hydrolysis process and 
playing a better “ pre-activation ” role. Similarly, compared with SUGPC- 
28 and SUGPC-40, DUGPC exhibits better capacitive performance 
( Fig. S4 & Table S4 ). As a result, DUGPC is selected for a comparative 
study with CGPC-50 and GPC as the control group to further explore its 
structure-performance relationship. Scheme 1 illustrates the whole 
evolution of garlic peel-based PC prepared by dual-frequency ultrasonic- 
assisted enzymolysis strategy.
3.2. Morphology and composition characterization of PCs
The intermediate products and final morphology of all PC samples 
were observed by SEM ( Fig. 1 & Fig. S5 ). As illustrated in Fig. S5 a, the 
garlic peel still maintains its original bundle structure after carboniza -
tion, and the supporting role of cellulose is not significantly affected. 
However, after pretreatment with cellulase, part of the cellulose was 
hydrolyzed into small molecule compounds and lost to the outside of the 
cell wall, so the bundle structure of the carbonized products shrank and 
some pores were created on the surface ( Fig. S5 b). When dual-frequency 
ultrasound is applied, the binding of cellulase to the substrate is 
enhanced, and the enhanced cavitation effect of ultrasound itself “ cuts ” 
the cell wall, resulting in partial damage to the tube bundle structure of 
the final carbonized product and more uniform dense pores on the 
surface ( Fig. S5 c).
Thus, GPC ( Fig. 1 a & Fig. S5 d) still partially retains the bundle 
structure and has a limited number of pores compared with CGPC-50 
( Fig. 1 b & Fig. S5 e), which can be inferred that cellulase treatment 
promotes the alkali-carbon fusion in the impregnation process and im -
proves the subsequent KOH pore-making efficiency. Although both have 
hierarchical pore structures, DUGPC ( Fig. 1 c & Fig. S5 f) is significantly 
more uniform and regular than CGPC-50, indicating that the process of 
dual-frequency ultrasound-assisted enzymolysis plays an ideal “ pre- 
activation ” role. In addition, TEM images of DUGPC observed at 
different magnifications are shown in Fig. 1 (d – f), confirming the hier -
archical pore distribution and nearly transparent sheet-like structure of 
DUGPC. The high-resolution image in Fig. 1 g further reveals the exis -
tence of high-density micropores in DUGPC and the disordered lattice 
streaks of graphite microcrystals, while the EDS element mapping in 
Fig. 1 h illustrates the uniform distribution of C, O and N.
